name: The Evens
label: Dischord
lede: Ian MacKaye turned the volume down, sat behind a baritone guitar across from Amy Farina's drums, and found out a punk band could play a barn, a museum or a theater lobby and still hit harder than most bands with a wall of amps.

eras.title: Two people, one quiet room
eras.text: Ian MacKaye had spent two decades at the loud end of Washington music, from Minor Threat to Fugazi. With Amy Farina, drummer in The Warmers, he started something built on restraint: one baritone guitar, one drum kit, two voices trading lines.

years.h: Ian MacKaye on baritone guitar, Amy Farina on drums
years.p: [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] and [[Amy Farina|30d1b9a6-4156-49ec-84ba-65c3f5ebbf69]] start playing together in Washington as the Evens. Dischord's description is plain: he plays baritone guitar, she plays drums, they both sing.
years.xp:
The Evens took shape as [[Fugazi|233fc3f3-6de2-465c-985e-e721dbabbace]] was winding down its touring life; Fugazi played its last shows in 2002 and went on what its members have always called an indefinite hiatus. The Evens were the opposite machine: no bass, no second guitar, and a volume level that let the words through.

Farina came up in [[The Warmers|af0dea4e-c501-47f2-8695-129f254d425f]] with Ian's brother [[Alec MacKaye|bb05a948-ea44-4c9b-9d19-2a48f757ca22]]. MacKaye and Farina were also a couple, and later married. The band and the household were the same two people, which shaped everything that came after.

years.h: The Evens' first release is a kids' TV video
years.p: Before the Evens had a record out, Ian MacKaye and Amy Farina made a video for their song Vowel Movement for Pancake Mountain, the D.C. internet children's show.

eras.title: Turn it down, play anywhere
eras.text: The Evens released two records in twenty months, The Evens and Get Evens, and toured outside the club circuit. Playing quiet meant Ian MacKaye and Amy Farina could set up in galleries, barns and lobbies, rooms where the audience actually had to listen.

years.h: The Evens, recorded at Inner Ear · Dischord No. 150
years.p: The Evens' debut, cut at Inner Ear in June 2004 with [[Don Zientara|a495882b-4585-4295-9269-e30c63f279fe]]: twelve songs, 37 minutes, a caged elephant silhouette on the cover.
years.xp:
Ian MacKaye and Amy Farina co-produced the record themselves with Zientara, who had engineered Dischord bands since the label's first days. The cover photo is by Lely Constantinople, with art by [[Jason Farrell|f458f662-c72b-485b-9152-81eda8659fdb]].

The Washington Post filed it under post-post-hardcore; AllMusic heard a major leap for MacKaye.

q: Turning down allowed us to play basically anywhere.
years.h: The Evens play barns, museums, galleries and lobbies
years.p: The Evens tour rooms most punk bands never see: barns, museums, art galleries, theater lobbies. Ian MacKaye told NPR the low volume was the whole point.
years.xp:
MacKaye has said that for most of his career the only rooms that would book his music were bars, rooms whose economy, as he put it, runs largely on self-destruction. Turning down freed the band from that. In a strange room, he told NPR, the music has to rise to meet it.

Over the following years the band toured Europe, South America, Oceania, Canada and the United States, according to Dischord.

years.h: Get Evens, recorded in the Dischord House basement
years.p: For their second album the Evens skipped the studio and recorded in the basement of the Dischord House in Arlington. Dischord released it as No. 160.
years.xp:
The Evens mixed Get Evens at Inner Ear with Don Zientara. Ten songs, from Cut From the Cloth to Dinner With the President.

Pitchfork gave it 7.8; Mojo, Spin and Uncut all came in positive. The LP was re-cut in 2010.

eras.title: A band that is also a family
eras.text: Ian MacKaye and Amy Farina's son arrived in 2008 and the Evens' clock changed. When both parents are the whole band, rehearsal, touring and bedtime all come out of the same calendar, and six years passed between Get Evens and The Odds.

years.h: Ian MacKaye and Amy Farina's son is born
years.p: Ian MacKaye and Amy Farina have a son. The Evens keep going, at a pace set by family life.

years.h: 2 Songs, the Evens' only single · Dischord No. 170
years.p: A seven-dollar seven-inch: Warble Factor backed with Timothy Wright, recorded at Inner Ear that August. Both songs turn up again on The Odds a year later.
years.xp: The Evens produced the session themselves, and [[TJ Lipple|ed4cd729-b4d2-4016-a0b6-c362b68d2afb]] mastered it.

q: He does like our music; he's also not too shy to critique things.
years.h: The Odds, the Evens' third album, after six years
years.p: Thirteen songs, opening with King of Kings and closing with a reprise called KOK. Metacritic logged universal acclaim, Pitchfork gave it 8.0, and Stereogum put it at No. 45 on its albums of 2012.
years.xp:
Critics heard parenthood all through The Odds. AllMusic's Fred Thomas called the record refined and understated. Not every song landed: several reviewers singled out Competing With the Till as the clumsy one.

Talking to NPR that winter, Amy Farina was frank about the logistics of a two-parent band, and said she and Ian MacKaye were lucky to have family nearby. Their four-year-old son, she added, was a fan with opinions.

eras.title: The duo grows a bass player
eras.text: After The Odds (2012), the Evens went quiet on record. Ian MacKaye and Amy Farina didn't stop playing, though: they started jamming with Joe Lally, MacKaye's old Fugazi bandmate, and that trio became Coriky.

years.h: Coriky, the Evens plus Joe Lally, release Coriky
years.p: Ian MacKaye and Amy Farina began playing with former Fugazi bassist [[Joe Lally|62046ffd-7d76-476b-bee5-b281b7575c6c]] in 2015. The trio's debut, delayed from March by COVID-19, came out on Dischord in June 2020.
years.xp: The Odds (2012) remains the most recent Evens record.

sources.title: NPR: The Evens, The Power Of Turning Down The Volume (2012)
